On 13 April 1919, British Indian troops under Brigadier General Reginald Dyer opened fire on an unarmed crowd in the Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar, Punjab. The crowd had gathered on the spring festival of Baisakhi to protest the arrest of two local leaders and the Rowlatt Act, which allowed detention without trial.

Dyer sent no warning and blocked the narrow exits. His men fired about 1,650 rounds into the crowd for roughly ten minutes. The British count was 379 dead, while Indian estimates were over 1,000.

Dyer had earlier banned all gatherings and then enforced martial law with public floggings and a "crawling order". He was removed from command, but many in Britain praised him. Poet Rabindranath Tagore gave back his knighthood in protest.

The massacre destroyed many Indians' trust in British rule. Gandhi turned from cooperating with the Raj to the non-cooperation movement of 1920, and the Congress took a harder line. In 1940 Udham Singh shot the former Punjab governor Michael O'Dwyer in London, in revenge.
